notes/1.1-stem-cell,-synthetic-biology-a.title: 1.1 Stem Cell, Synthetic Biology and Biomaterial Innovations for MPS
notes/1.1-stem-cell,-synthetic-biology-a.content:
Nicholas Kurniawan, Eindhoven University of Technology
Probing the dynamics of cell mechanosensing using photoresponsive materials
Great talk on mechanosensing, addressing the key question of how cells are able to sense curvature and how they respond to it. Showed some ways of biofabricating these surfaces with e.g. the intended groove size to test mechanosensitivity.
Later, I had a chat with him during one of the breaks.
Antonio J. Ortega (U Maryland)
Engineering vision in vitro: Functional light-evoked responses from retinal organoids
This was purely focussed on retinal organoids and rather specific. The speaker claims that human retinal organoids do not sufficiently recapitulate biology, but by switching to another animal (some monkey?) that has a slightly different set of cone and rod cells, they were able to engineer retinal organoids that more closely resemble actual biology.
Marta Sacchi, University Grenoble Alpes, CEA,
Engineering programmable mechanical and electrical microenvironments for brain organoid systems
This talk focussed on a method to produce “synthetic ECM” that does not have the disadvantages of Matrigel (similar to what Eugi from Victor Peperzak’s group is doing). However, the rest of the talk was very much focussed on brain organoids so I’m not sure how general their method is.


Tamara Rossy, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Tissue engineering mature and functional 2.5D models of the human neuromuscular interface from iPSCs

notes/keynote.title: Keynote
notes/keynote.content:
Catalyzing Innovation and Accelerating Impact in Human-Based Science
Nicole Kleinstreuer
Explanation of the NIH and especially the division responsible for developing and regulating MPS. Overall strategy to further develop animal free testing to speed up drug development.
She also emphasized multiple times the importance of integrating AI and computational models into MPS development.



Human Organs Chips for Disease Modeling, Drug Development, and Personalized Medicine
(Donald E. Ingber, Wyss Institute)
Father of the organ-on-a-chip field. Large overview of probably >40 OoC projects Donald Ingber worked on (one project per slide), showing the overall development of the field over the last years.
Designing High Throughput MPS for Vascularized Organoids: Using Patient-Derived Organoids for IND Filing (Noo Li Jeon, Seoul National University)
Expert on vascularization, also founded a cool company called Qureator with highly automated labs and workflows.
Artificial and Biological Intelligence for Precision Oncology (Fanny Jaulin, Gustave Roussy)
Despite the title, not an AI talk but more focussed on organoids. However, they developed a huge database of apparently millions of organoid experiments (imaging?) which they used to train an AI model for personalized medicine.
Paving the Way for Personalized Medicine in Space and on Earth (Lisa Carnell, NASA)
NASA is advancing human health in space through next-generation biological platforms. Aboard Artemis II was a first-of-its-kind study using microphysiological systems to study the effects of deep-space stressors on astronaut health. During her keynote, Dr. Carnell will provide an overview of the AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) investigation, which is a collaboration between NASA, other government agencies, and industry. She will discuss how this research could enable precision health benefitting future missions to the Moon and Mars, as well as patient treatments on Earth.
Light-hearted fun talk from NASA where they described some experiments bringing cells and organoids into space.

notes/run-club.title: Run club
notes/run-club.content:
Meeting Location: The corner of 9th St NW and K St NW
Map Route and Directions Below
Start your day with fresh air and great company by joining fellow conference attendees for the Morning Run Group. This informal meet-up offers a chance to get moving before the day’s sessions begin while connecting with others in the community who enjoy running.
Participants will gather in the morning for a group run at a comfortable, conversational pace. Whether you are a regular runner or simply looking for an energizing way to begin the day, all experience levels are welcome.
The run is a casual, participant/self-led activity intended to encourage wellness and networking outside the formal conference program. Attendees are encouraged to bring appropriate running gear and join for as much or as little of the run as they wish.
Run Directions: 2.69 miles

Start at the corner of 9th St NW and K St NW
Head south on 9th St NW toward the National Mall
Turn left onto the National Mall path
Continue east, then turn left onto 3rd St SW
Turn left onto Pennsylvania Ave NW
Turn right onto 7th St NW
Turn left onto K St NW to complete the run
